name: The Venetian Macao
label: Venetian Macao
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lord Stow's Bakery' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Lord Stow’s Bakery' (node/5606474821): point; moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1156708: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Giant resort with indoor canals and gondolas, on Cotai.

text.description: The Venetian Macao is a huge hotel and casino resort on the Cotai Strip, modelled on its sister resort in Las Vegas. The main tower has 39 storeys and the resort opened on 28 August 2007. Inside there are around 300 shops and an indoor canal, which is what makes it so photogenic: the corridors look like a Venetian street, with a painted sky overhead. This spot's photo is taken indoors, from the small bridge on the 2nd floor beside Lord Stow's Bakery. Look diagonally down the corridor and you get a long, nearly empty view with the painted-sky light falling through the space. One guide suggests it as a quieter alternative to the busy bridge over the Grand Canal. The resort is very large, so allow time to find your way inside. The exterior of the building doesn't appear in this view. If you want the canal, Grand Canal Shoppes shows a gondola under the painted sky with the Venetian-style facades behind it. For a night-time frame of the lit frontage and the red buses, try Starlight Bridge. For the corridor shot, stand still, keep the phone level and let the perspective do the work. Shoot a few frames with and without people walking through, then pick the cleanest.
text.geographic_location: On the Cotai Strip, built on reclaimed land, in the Cotai area of Macau, among a group of large resorts.
text.directions_text: Head for the Cotai Strip resort area and look for The Venetian Macao. The resort also runs its own private buses, and Cotai West station on the Macau LRT is within reach. Once inside, make your way to the 2nd floor and look for Lord Stow's Bakery; the small bridge is beside it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view down the corridor. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the ceiling and the full sweep of the space, but keep the phone level so the lines don't lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (small bridge on the 2nd floor beside the bakery; shoot diagonally down the corridor). A diagonal view down a nearly empty interior corridor, with the fake-sky light falling through the space.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Aim diagonally down the corridor rather than straight along it, so the lines lead the eye into the picture. Switch on gridlines and use them to keep the verticals straight. If you also want the canal, Grand Canal Shoppes is the alternative viewpoint, with a gondola under the painted sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bright painted sky to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the colours stay rich and the ceiling isn't washed out. Hold the phone steady with both hands; if night mode switches on in dim areas, stay still until it finishes.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around 4 PM, when sunlight shines through the painted sky.

text.access_note: The resort is a commercial complex with shops, a casino and an arena, so check the official site before you go for any access rules.
claims_not_in_sources: The shopping areas of the resort are normally open to visitors, but some areas (such as the casino) may have their own rules.
Photographing with people walking through the corridor is likely, so waiting for a gap can help.
Dim indoor light can make a phone switch on night mode automatically.

name: Grand Lisboa
label: Grand Lisboa
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rua Nova à Guia' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '東望洋新街 Rua Nova à Guia' (way/1033527359): middle (106 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/192182404: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Grand Lisboa' (157 m across).

text.description:
The Grand Lisboa is a 47-floor, 261-metre hotel tower in Sé, and it is the tallest building in Macau. Its casino and restaurants opened in February 2007 and the hotel followed in December 2008. It was designed by the Hong Kong architects Dennis Lau and Ng Chun Man. It is the most distinctive part of Macau's skyline.

The best-known phone photo is taken from Rua Nova à Guia. From the left-hand pavement, the tower rises above low, older residential buildings along the street. That mix of old and new is what makes this the classic postcard view of the hotel. Several guides call it the signature Grand Lisboa shot, and one says the left side of the road gives the best angle.

The street is residential and the traffic is heavy, so stay on the pavement and never step into the road to line up a shot. Start with the default lens (1x) and let the street lead the eye towards the tower. If the top is cut off, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) or step back along the pavement. Early morning is quieter and the sun is less harsh, though another guide finds the afternoon light kinder.

If you want a different view, Guia Hill Municipal Park gives an elevated panorama over the peninsula. Nam Van Lake shows the tower across the water, often with city lights reflected in it.
text.geographic_location: The Grand Lisboa is in Sé, on the Macau Peninsula.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, rail or tram stops listed nearby, so make your way to the Grand Lisboa in Sé on foot or by a ride of your choice, or to the Mei Ka Building, which some guides use as the navigation target for the street. From the Grand Lisboa, head north-east to Rua Nova à Guia, about 430 m on foot. Walk on the left-hand pavement and look back towards the south-west to see the tower. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x). Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the top of the tower is cut off, or the telephoto (2x or more) to bring the tower closer above the older buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rua Nova à Guia (left-hand sidewalk, with the hotel behind you; one guide says Mei Ka Building is the navigation target). The Grand Lisboa tower rises above low, older residential buildings along the street, creating the old-versus-new contrast that makes this the classic postcard frame. Keep to the pavement because the traffic is heavy.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the tower on one of the vertical lines. Let the street and the older buildings fill the lower part of the frame, so the old-versus-new contrast is clear. If you want another angle, Guia Hill Municipal Park or Nam Van Lake also show the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out. Wipe the lens first, then take a few frames between passing vehicles.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is quieter for traffic and the sun is gentler. One guide finds the afternoon light favourable, so you could try both.

text.access_note: Rua Nova à Guia is an ordinary public street with no entry fee, but it is busy with traffic. For the hotel and casino themselves, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Looking south-west from the stand-here point, the morning sun is behind or to the side of you, so the tower is lit rather than backlit.
Wiping the phone lens before shooting helps keep the picture sharp.

name: Macau Tower
label: Macau Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Nam Van Lake' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '南灣湖 Lago Nam Van' (relation/7588101): edge nearest the subject (1195 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/7914304898: the OpenStreetMap point 'Macau Tower'.
notes: 338 m tower with observation deck and skywalk.

text.description:
Macau Tower is the tall, slim tower on the southern side of the Macau peninsula. It stands 338 m high and is used for viewing, entertainment, telecommunications and broadcasting. It was opened on 19 December 2001 and was inspired by the Sky Tower in Auckland, New Zealand. It sits on land created by the Nam Van reclamation project, which added 130 hectares and made the peninsula about 20% bigger.

It photographs well because its shape is simple and clear against the sky, and the open water in front of it gives you room to step back and fit it all in. The best-known place to shoot it is the lakeside promenade at Nam Van Lake. The tower rises above the lake and the waterfront skyline, and on calm evenings the lights are often reflected in the water. As you walk along the promenade the tower stays in view, so you can try several angles before choosing one.

For a phone, turn the phone upright (portrait) so the full height fits, and keep some water in the bottom of the frame for the reflection. Wait for a moment when the surface is still. If you want a different view, Sai Van Bridge shows the tower framed by its reflection in the still lake water beside the bridge, and the Chapel of Our Lady of Penha gives a wider view across the hill and lakes with the tower in the distance. The promenade is the easiest option.
text.geographic_location: Macau Tower is in the Sé area of the Macau peninsula, on reclaimed land in the Nam Van area. The lakeside promenade where you take the photo is a short walk to the north-east, facing the tower across the water.
text.directions_text: Head for the Nam Van area on the southern side of the Macau peninsula and use a map app to reach Nam Van Lake or Macau Tower. Walk along the lakeside promenade with the tower behind you, then turn round to take the photo. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to see the tower with the lake and skyline around it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more water and reflection, or to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the tower's shape against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Nam Van Lake (lakeside promenade facing the tower). The tower rising above the lake and the waterfront skyline, often with reflections in the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright and turn on gridlines so the tower stands straight against a vertical line. Leave a band of water along the bottom to catch the reflection. If you have time, Sai Van Bridge or the Chapel of Our Lady of Penha give different views of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on a railing or hold your breath as you shoot to avoid blur. Tap the tower to focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down so the tower lights do not blow out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset or after dark, when the tower and skyline lights are on and the reflections are strongest.

text.access_note: The lakeside promenade is a free, open public space; the tower's observation deck and activities are ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Wynn Macau
label: Wynn Macau
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rua Cidade de Sintra' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '仙德麗街 Rua Cidade de Sintra' (way/820474487): point nearest the subject (152 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/192179929: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Wynn' (159 m across).
notes: Resort known for its fountain and Performance Lake show.

text.description: Wynn Macau is a luxury hotel and casino resort on the Macau Peninsula. It opened on 6 September 2006 and has two towers. The second, Encore, opened on 21 April 2010, and together they hold 1,008 rooms and suites. What makes it good for phone photos is the lake in front of the building. On a calm evening the building is reflected almost in full, so you get the real tower and a mirror image in one frame. The hotel is at its best in the blue hour after sunset or at night, when the lights come on. A guide for photographers says this side is also quiet, with very few other people around. Keep the lake edge level in your frame and let the reflection fill the lower half. If you want a different mood, Nam Van Lake Square is another option for a wide lakeside sunset view. It looks towards the Macau Tower and is not framed on Wynn Macau. Wait a moment between shots if the surface is rippling, because the reflection often sharpens again once the water settles.
text.geographic_location: On the Macau Peninsula, along Rua Cidade de Sintra, on the lakeside directly opposite the Wynn Macau resort.
text.directions_text: Check its exact position on the map before you set out. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the whole building and its reflection fit in one frame. If the towers are cut off at the top or sides, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) and keep the phone level so the edges do not lean. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the lit facade or a slice of the reflection.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rua Cidade de Sintra (opposite the Wynn hotel, at the lakeside). The Wynn Macau building reflected almost fully in the lake in front of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the lake edge on the lower third line, so the building fills the upper part and the reflection fills the lower part. Hold the phone low and straight-on so the reflection lines up with the tower. For a different view, Nam Van Lake Square gives an open lakeside scene with sunset over the water and the Macau Tower, rather than a picture of Wynn Macau.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the bright lights do not wash out. At night, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on a wall or railing, or hold your breath as you shoot, to keep the image sharp. Take a few frames, because ripples change the reflection from one shot to the next.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour, just after sunset, or at night, when the building is lit and the reflection stands out most.

text.access_note: The lakeside street is a public place with no payment needed, but check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside the resort.
claims_not_in_sources: A calm water surface gives the clearest reflection, and wind ripples can break it up.
The hotel is lit after dark, which strengthens the reflection at blue hour and at night.
Resting your elbows on a wall or railing helps keep night photos steady.

name: Senado Square
label: Senado Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Leal Senado' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '市政署大樓 Edifício do Leal Senado' (way/192573674): middle (92 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/192573684: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Senado Square' (131 m across).
notes: Wave-patterned pavement square surrounded by pastel colonial buildings.

text.description: Senado Square is the paved, pedestrian-only heart of old Macau, and part of the UNESCO Historic Centre of Macau. It is an elongated triangle of about 3,700 square metres, linking Avenida de Almeida Ribeiro at one end with Largo do São Domingos at the other. The square is named after the Leal Senado, where Chinese and Portuguese met between the 16th and 18th centuries. Most of the buildings around it are European in style and many are protected monuments. They include the Holy House of Mercy, Hotel Central and the General Post Office. The whole area was covered in Portuguese pavement in the early 1990s and closed to traffic, and the wave-patterned paving now leads the eye towards the colonial facades. That is what makes it work on a phone: strong leading lines, pastel buildings and plenty of depth. Start with the cream-white front of the Leal Senado with its green doors and windows, then turn to look along the whole square, with the fountain in the middle and St. Dominic's Church in the distance. For a quieter backdrop, the narrow Travessa da Misericórdia nearby has bright yellow facades and colourful shutters. Expect crowds, especially at weekends, on public holidays and from about 8 AM. Some buildings have been under renovation, with green netting over a few walls, and the fountain is sometimes switched off, so don't count on either. The square is also decorated for the December Light Festival and Chinese New Year.
text.geographic_location: Senado Square is in the Sé district, part of the UNESCO Historic Centre of Macau, beside the Leal Senado and the Holy House of Mercy. It runs between Avenida de Almeida Ribeiro and Largo do São Domingos.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot, so use a map app to reach Largo do Senado (Senado Square) in the Sé area, the old centre of Macau. The square is pedestrian-only, so you will finish on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the front of the Leal Senado, as it looks natural and keeps the building's lines straight. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want the whole square and the paving in one frame. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as the green doors and windows or the church in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Leal Senado (front facade, facing the square). Eye-level frontal view of the cream-white Leal Senado facade with its green doors and windows, framed by the square. For a wider view of the whole square, look along it from its south end, where the wave-pattern paving runs towards the colonial facades, the fountain and St. Dominic's Church.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the facade up square to the frame, holding the phone level so the building doesn't lean. Keep the paving in the lower part of the picture so its waves lead the eye in. For a quieter shot, walk into Travessa da Misericórdia and use its yellow facades and shutters as a backdrop. A low-angle side view of the Leal Senado also works.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the cream-white walls keep their detail. If green netting covers part of a wall, try a tighter telephoto frame or a different angle. Live Photos can be handy for catching people crossing the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before about 8 AM, when the square is quietest. Weekends and public holidays are very crowded. During the December Light Festival and Chinese New Year the decorations add colour.

text.access_note: Senado Square is an open, pedestrian-only public space; the Leal Senado and Holy House of Mercy are part of a historic site where visitors are asked to stay quiet and respectful, and for any building interiors check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Cream-white walls can lose detail in bright light, so lowering the exposure slider slightly helps.
Tilting the phone upwards makes building lines lean inwards, so holding it level keeps them straighter.
A tighter telephoto frame can leave out netting or scaffolding on parts of a wall.

name: Ruins of St. Paul's
label: Ruins of St. Paul's
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Largo da Companhia de Jesus' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '耶穌會紀念廣場 Largo da Companhia de Jesus' (way/710516681): middle (39 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/192183185: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ruins of St. Paul' (21 m across).
notes: Facade of the 17th-century Jesuit church, the symbol of Macau.

text.description: The Ruins of St. Paul's are what is left of a 17th-century Jesuit church and college in the Santo António area of Macau: a tall carved stone façade standing at the top of a wide staircase. The Jesuits built the complex between 1602 and 1640, and it was among the largest Catholic churches in Asia at the time. A fire during a typhoon on 26 January 1835 destroyed everything except the front. It photographs well because the façade stands alone against the sky, with 68 stone steps leading up to it, so the whole scene has a clear shape and a strong sense of height. Look closely at the carvings: they show the Assumption of Mary and mix in Asian touches, such as Mary treading on a seven-headed hydra, and six Chinese guardian lions are carved at the base. The ruins are part of the Historic Centre of Macau, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. For the classic photo, stand in the square at the foot of the staircase and shoot the whole façade rising above the steps. For a second view, try Travessa da Paixão, where the façade appears at the end of a narrow cobbled lane between pastel townhouses. Another is the Fortaleza do Monte, which looks down on the ruins with the city skyline behind. Go early if you can, as the steps and square fill up with visitors later in the day.
text.geographic_location: In the Santo António area of the Macau Peninsula, at the top of a staircase of 68 stone steps above Largo da Companhia de Jesus, with the Fortaleza do Monte on the hill above.
text.directions_text: Head for the Santo António area of the Macau Peninsula; the Chinese name is 大三巴牌坊. Walk up to the square and the foot of the staircase, then look up at the front. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the whole façade and the staircase in one frame. If the square is busy or you cannot step back far enough, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the carvings and the guardian lions.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Largo da Companhia de Jesus (foot of the staircase, centre of the square). The full stone façade rising above the staircase, framed by the plaza and the stairs leading up to it. If you want a different view, try Travessa da Paixão, where the façade appears at the top of a narrow cobbled lane, or the Fortaleza do Monte for a view down onto the ruins.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the façade up with the vertical lines so the stonework does not lean. Keep the staircase in the lower part of the frame to show the height. Hold the phone level, because tilting it upwards makes the façade lean backwards. For a second shot, use the lane at Travessa da Paixão, where the pastel houses and balconies frame the façade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pale stone to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out the carving detail. Photography is restricted inside the façade and the museum behind it, so take your main shots from the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, around 07:30 to 08:30, is suggested for cleaner, less crowded frames. Light can vary, so check it on the day.

text.access_note: The façade and the square in front can be seen from outside, but photography is restricted inside the museum behind it. The Macao Museum at the Fortaleza do Monte charges an admission fee, so check the official site before you go.

name: A-Ma Temple
label: A-Ma Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Largo do Pagode da Barra' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '媽閣廟前地 Largo do Pagode da Barra' (relation/18544991): middle (119 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/192187333: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'A-Ma Temple' (48 m across).
notes: Ancient waterfront temple dedicated to the sea goddess Mazu.

text.description:
A-Ma Temple is a working temple to the sea-goddess Mazu, and one of the oldest in Macau. It was built in 1488, and the name Macau is thought to come from it. It is part of the Historic Centre of Macau, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005. The complex has six main parts, including a gate pavilion, a memorial arch, a prayer hall and the Hall of Benevolence, its oldest section.

For a phone photo, the best first shot is the entrance. From Largo do Pagode da Barra, the square in front, you see the red-and-grey gate with its green-glazed roof edges and guardian lions, set against a wooded slope. Mosaic pavement and older façades sit at the edges of the frame, which gives the picture a sense of place. Take that wide view first, showing the gate and the hillside together, then move in for details such as roof ends and lions.

The temple is still used for worship, so be discreet around people praying. Photography is generally fine outdoors but not inside the halls, and flash and tripods are not welcome in worship areas. If you want a second view, the temple's stacked roofs look out over the inner harbour from inside the grounds, and the Chapel of Our Lady of Penha gives a wider skyline view after a short uphill walk.
text.geographic_location: A-Ma Temple is in the São Lourenço area of Macau, at the foot of a wooded slope with the inner harbour beyond.
text.directions_text: No tram or station stop is listed for this spot, so head for the São Lourenço area of Macau. Ask for A-Ma Temple or Largo do Pagode da Barra (Barra Square, 妈阁前地). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the gate, the roof edges and the wooded slope into one frame. Then use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the gate. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof ornaments and the lions without walking into worshippers' space.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Largo do Pagode da Barra (Barra Square (妈阁前地), facing the vermilion main gate from across the square; step back before the gate). The red-and-grey temple gate with its green-glazed roof edges and guardian lions, set against the wooded slope, with colonial façades and mosaic pavement at the edges of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the gate on the centre line, with the hillside above it. Include a strip of mosaic pavement at the bottom so the square leads the eye to the gate. Take this whole-scene shot first, then move closer for details. For another view, the Chapel of Our Lady of Penha, a short uphill walk away, looks over the skyline of the peninsula.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the red paint stays rich and the sky does not wash out. Turn the flash off, and do not use a tripod near worship areas.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Arrive between 7 and 9 AM for soft light and fewer crowds. Sunset light also suits the gate. Expect the biggest crowds during the Tin Hau Festival.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship; the square outside is open, but check the official site before you go for entry rules, and do not photograph inside the halls.

name: Macau Fisherman's Wharf
label: Fisherman's Wharf
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Macau Fisherman's Wharf' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Macau Fisherman's Wharf'.
notes: Themed waterfront park with a Roman amphitheatre and a volcano.

text.description: Macau Fisherman's Wharf is a themed waterfront complex in Sé, built in the style of different world seaports, with Cape Town and Amsterdam among the examples. It has over 70 shops and restaurants, a marina, two hotels and a casino. It officially opened on 31 December 2006. For photographs, the best-known feature is the Roman-style amphitheatre, a replica of the Colosseum with stone arches, columns and steps. It is the strongest backdrop in the complex because it is large, simple in shape and looks good against open sky. The amphitheatre is a venue for concerts and other performances and is usually closed, so you photograph it from outside the arches and columns. That works well on a phone. Stand back far enough to see the full curve of the arches, then step in close for a frame of columns and sky. The complex also has a Potala Palace replica on an artificial volcano and a Victorian-style hotel, which give you more shots if you have time. Many shops and restaurants have been reported closed on some visits, so expect a quiet, open feel rather than a bustling one. If you want a second view, the colourful European-style buildings of the harbourfront at Lai Chun Wharf show the sea, the Friendship Bridge in the distance and sometimes the Macau Tower in one frame.
text.geographic_location: Macau Fisherman's Wharf is on the waterfront in the Sé district of Macau, on land partly reclaimed from the sea. The Roman-style amphitheatre stands near the entrance to the complex.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot, so check a map app for the best way to reach the wharf. Navigate to Macau Fisherman's Wharf (Doca dos Pescadores, 澳門漁人碼頭). Once inside, walk to the amphitheatre area near the entrance and stand outside the arches and columns, where the phone icon on the map is. The phone icon on the map is about 150 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole amphitheatre. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close and want all the arches and steps in one frame. If you stand further back, telephoto (2x-5x) is good for tight shots of the stone columns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 150 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. At Macau Fisherman's Wharf, on the Roman-style amphitheatre side near the entrance, outside the arches and columns. From here you see the Colosseum-style replica with its stone arches, columns and steps against open sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines so they do not lean. Keep plenty of sky in the frame. Hold the phone low and tilt it slightly upwards for height, but keep the grid level. If you also visit Lai Chun Wharf, use the default lens (1x) to get the coloured buildings, the sea and the distant bridge in one picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the stone is not washed out. After sunset, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a wall, because the phone needs to stay still for a few seconds.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before and after sunset, when the light is soft and warm on the stone.

text.access_note: The wharf is a commercial district and the amphitheatre is usually closed, so photograph it from outside; check the official site before you go for what is open.

name: Fortaleza do Monte
label: Monte Fort
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fortaleza do Monte' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/46510080: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fortaleza do Monte' (180 m across).
notes: Hilltop fort with cannons and views over the old town.

text.description: Fortaleza do Monte is the old hilltop fort that once guarded Macau, and it is one of the best places in the city to take photos of the city itself. The cannons still point out over the rooftops, and the tree-covered park on top gives you shade and space to wander. The best-known angle is from the south-west battlements, looking down the slope. From there you see the back of the Ruins of St. Paul's façade, with its iron supports showing, and the city spreading out behind it. Most visitors photograph that landmark from the steps in front, so this view feels fresh. The fort was built between 1617 and 1626 on a hill about 52 metres high, directly east of the Ruins of St. Paul's, to protect the Jesuits' property from pirates. It helped hold off a Dutch attempt to invade in 1622. It covers roughly 8,000 square metres, and thirty-two cannon were placed around its walls. It opened to the public in 1965 and now houses the Museum of Macau. There are two other good photos up here. One is the old cannons in the foreground with the Grand Lisboa and the dense rooftops of the peninsula behind. The other is the garden and walls with trees and benches, where you can often frame fewer people. Go early if you can, as morning light is cleaner on the façade.
text.geographic_location: In the Santo António area of the Macau Peninsula, on a hill directly east of the Ruins of St. Paul's.
text.directions_text: Head to the Ruins of St. Paul's first, then walk east up the hill to the fort, which stands on the hill directly east of the Ruins. Check the official site for the current entrance arrangements before you go. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the wide city view. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the fort walls and garden, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the façade of the Ruins of St. Paul's from the battlements.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there, walk to the south-west battlements of Fortaleza do Monte and look down the slope. From the battlements you see the back of the Ruins of St. Paul's façade below, with its iron supports visible, and the city spreading out behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the façade on one of the lower thirds, with the rooftops filling the rest of the frame. Keep the edge of the battlement wall in the corner to give the shot depth. For a second picture, crouch beside an old cannon and frame it in the foreground with the Grand Lisboa behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out. Keep your phone steady against the wall for sharper telephoto shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning before about 10am, when the light hits the façade from the east and gives clean shadows. By midday the light is flat.

text.access_note: The grounds and battlements are open to the public, but the Macau Museum inside the fort may charge admission and opening times vary, so check the official site before you go.

name: St. Dominic's Church, Macau
label: St. Dominic's Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Largo do Senado' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '議事亭前地 Largo do Senado' (way/192573684): middle (131 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/192573688: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. Dominic's Church' (67 m across).
notes: Yellow baroque church with a cream-and-white interior.

text.description:
St. Dominic's Church is a Baroque church with a yellow façade, green shutters and white trim, standing at the edge of Senado Square in the old centre of Macau. The Dominican friars finished it in 1587, though the building you see today dates from the early 17th century after rebuilding. It is part of the Historic Centre of Macau, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The design mixes European and local touches, such as Chinese-style roof tiles and teak doors. A sacred art museum sits in the bell tower.

It photographs well because of its setting. The colour stands out against the busy square, and the wave-pattern paving, passers-by, umbrellas and bicycles all help lead the eye towards the building. Rather than a tight shot of the façade, try a wider, more relaxed picture that shows the church as part of the square. That is also an easy way to add it to your photos of Senado Square.

The church was reported closed for renovation in late 2024, so scaffolding or barriers may affect the view. Check when you arrive, and please stay behind any closure lines. The square can be crowded, so an early start gives you the cleanest frame. If you want the façade on its own, walk up to Largo de São Domingos, where the paving makes a good foreground.
text.geographic_location: St. Dominic's Church is on the Macau peninsula, at Largo de São Domingos, right next to Senado Square and close to the Leal Senado Building.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Senado Square area in the old centre of the peninsula. Walk towards the yellow building at the top of the square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the church within the square. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the crowds or the width of the square make it hard to fit everything in. Use the telephoto/zoom (2x-5x) for details such as the shutters and trim.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Largo do Senado (from the Senado Square side, looking toward the church). The church façade set within the wider square, with lines of the paving, passing people, umbrellas or bicycles leading the eye toward the yellow building.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the church off-centre, with the paving lines running towards it. Wait for a few people or a passing bicycle to add life to the foreground. For a tighter alternative, walk up to Largo de São Domingos and use the wave-pattern pavement as a foreground for the façade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the façade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the yellow stays rich and the sky does not wash out. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines stay straight, especially with ultra-wide.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is the best bet for fewer people in the square.

text.access_note: The square is open public space, but the church is a place of worship with a museum and may be closed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Guia Fortress
label: Guia Fortress
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Farol da Guia' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '東望洋燈塔 Farol da Guia' (way/230576208): middle (13 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/404669396: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Guia Fortress' (99 m across).
notes: Fort and 1865 lighthouse on the highest point of the peninsula.

text.description:
Guia Fortress sits on Guia Hill, the highest point on the Macau peninsula at about 91 metres. It is a complex of fort, chapel and lighthouse, and it is part of the UNESCO-listed Historic Centre of Macau. The fort and chapel were built between 1622 and 1638, and the fort was already partly built when the Dutch tried and failed to take Macau. The lighthouse followed in 1864-65 and is described as the first western-style lighthouse on the China coast. The chapel is Capela de Nossa Senhora da Guia, and frescoes with both western and Chinese themes were uncovered inside it in 1998.

For photographs, the best part is the summit, where the white lighthouse and the chapel stand side by side. The chapel's white wall and the lighthouse each make a clean backdrop, and the city and harbour spread out below. Stand on the open ground in front of the white walls and fit both buildings into the frame. If you walk over to the fortress ramparts, an old cannon can frame a wide view over the peninsula, with Taipa and Cotai to the south. Photography is not allowed inside the chapel, so take your pictures outside. Guides recommend late afternoon or sunset. The lighthouse is sometimes closed and the cable car does not run on Mondays, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Guia Fortress is on Guia Hill in the São Lázaro area of the Macau peninsula, on the highest ground in the city. The lighthouse and chapel stand together at the summit.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this hill. A cable car serves Guia Hill, but it does not run on Mondays. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the lighthouse, chapel and sky into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the white walls. From the ramparts, try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the harbour and distant buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (summit, lighthouse with the chapel beside it; shoot from the open ground in front of the white walls). The white lighthouse and chapel in the foreground, with the city and harbour spread out below on the hilltop.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the gridlines and place the lighthouse on one third of the frame, with the chapel's white wall beside it. Keep the phone level so the tower stays upright. For a second view, walk to the fortress ramparts, where an old cannon frames a wide panorama over the peninsula and south towards Taipa and Cotai.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white walls to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the walls keep their detail and don't turn pale. Panorama mode works well along the ramparts if you hold the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or sunset is recommended by guides. Some prefer the morning, so it's worth checking the sky on the day.

text.access_note: This is a heritage site with a chapel and lighthouse, and the lighthouse is sometimes closed and the cable car does not run on Mondays, so check the official site before you go.

name: Cathedral of the Nativity of Our Lady, Macau
label: Macau Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Largo da Sé' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '大堂前地 Largo da Sé' (way/306855650): middle (50 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/330368426: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sé Cathedral (Cathedral of the Nativity of Our Lady)' (72 m across).

text.description:
The Cathedral of the Nativity of Our Lady, known locally as Sé Catedral or Igreja da Sé, is the cathedral of the Diocese of Macau and part of the Historic Centre of Macau World Heritage Site. It began as a small wooden chapel in the early 1600s and became a cathedral in 1623. A stone church was consecrated in 1850, but a typhoon almost destroyed it 24 years later. The building you see today was rebuilt in concrete in 1937.

It photographs well because of the square in front of it. Largo da Sé gives you the Baroque facade framed by the colourful square, with a fountain and a row of benches in the foreground. The fountain and benches line up against the cathedral's bright wall, which is why this is the classic frame. The square is also fairly quiet, even though it is close to the busy streets around Senado Square, so you can usually take your time.

Stand in the square facing the church front and take a wide shot first, with the fountain and benches to give depth. Then move closer for a tighter shot of the facade. Keep your phone upright for the full height of the front, or turn it sideways to include more of the square. If you step inside, remember it is an active church. Photography inside is generally allowed, but use no flash, and be aware that visitors are discouraged during Sunday services.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral stands in the Sé area of the Macau peninsula, in the Historic Centre of Macau. It faces Largo da Sé, a short walk from the busy streets around Senado Square.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground or tram stops at this spot, so head for the Sé area, close to Senado Square. Ask for Largo da Sé or Sé Cathedral. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the facade, the fountain and the benches together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Largo da Sé (stand in the square facing the church front). The Baroque facade framed by the colourful square, with its fountain and a row of benches in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the fountain and benches up against the bright wall of the cathedral. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines of the facade stay straight. Take one wide shot with the foreground, then a tighter one of the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bright facade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the wall keeps its detail. If people walk through the frame, try a Live Photo and pick the cleanest moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the square is quiet. Avoid Sunday service times, when visitors are discouraged.

text.access_note: The cathedral is an active place of worship, so use no flash and avoid Sunday services; check the official site before you go for visiting times.

name: Na Tcha Temple
label: Na Tcha Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pátio do Espinho' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '茨林圍 Pátio do Espinho' (way/655138589): middle (174 m across).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Na Tcha Temple'.
notes: Small temple beside the Old City Wall next to St. Paul's.

text.description:
Na Tcha Temple is a very small Chinese folk religion temple, built in 1888 and dedicated to the deity Na Tcha. It is thought to have been raised to help end a plague that was troubling the area. It sits right behind the Ruins of St. Paul's, and in 2004 it became part of the Historic Centre of Macau, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The building is a single plain chamber, only 8.4 metres long and 4.51 metres wide, painted grey, with a gable roof about five metres high. Small ceramic animal figures sit along the ridge, and there are a few paintings on the walls under the entrance porch.

It photographs well because of the contrast. A tiny grey temple stands beside a surviving stretch of the old city wall, just behind the Ruins of St. Paul's. The best view is from Pátio do Espinho, a small courtyard inside the wall, reached by the passage beside the temple. From there the grey roof and stone walls fill the foreground, with the wall rising behind. A second option is Calçada de S. Francisco Xavier, where the two alleys meet. It shows the temple's front and entrance, with the stone facade of the ruins close behind.

The spaces are tight, so you will not need to walk far. Take a few frames from different heights and angles, and keep people out of the doorway if you can. This is a working place of worship, so be polite when photographing anyone inside.
text.geographic_location: In the Santo António area of Macau, directly behind the Ruins of St. Paul's. It stands where two small alleys meet, Rua da Ressurreição and Calçada de S. Francisco Xavier.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop nearby, so go to the Ruins of St. Paul's and walk round to the temple behind it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the temple, wall and roof together. In the narrow courtyard, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough. Keep it level and keep people away from the edges of the frame, as the ultra-wide stretches anything near the edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Pátio do Espinho (inside the old city wall, reached by the passage beside the temple). The small temple framed by the surviving section of the old city wall, with the grey roof and stone walls in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the roof line on a horizontal line, with the wall filling one side. Hold the phone low to emphasise the stone and the roof against the wall. For a second picture, walk to Calçada de S. Francisco Xavier, where the two alleys meet, for the temple's front and entrance with the ruins' stone facade just behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the grey wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky behind the roof looks washed out. Telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) is useful for the ridge figurines, but hold steady.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship in a heritage area, so be respectful and check the official site before you go for current access and visiting rules.

name: St. Lawrence's Church, Macau
label: St. Lawrence's Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Igreja de São Lourenço' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).

text.description:
St. Lawrence's Church (Igreja de São Lourenço) is one of the oldest churches in Macau. It was first built before 1560 by the Jesuits and rebuilt in 1846. The building you see today is neoclassical, with a yellow exterior and white details, and it is still a working Catholic church as well as a popular place to visit. Inside, the church is decorated with ornate pillars and chandeliers.

It photographs well because the front is so tidy. The yellow and white facade and the twin bell towers are almost perfectly symmetrical, and the stone staircase leads the eye up to the entrance. The stairs rise from Rua de São Lourenço into a palm garden, and the palms give you some green in the foreground. The classic shot is from the front steps, looking up at the entrance, which gives a raised, balanced view of the whole front. If you want the full facade and both towers in one frame, step back down to Rua de São Lourenço and shoot up at the church instead.

Aim for late afternoon, when the low sun warms the yellow walls. Sunday Mass is held here, so keep your voice down and be considerate of worshippers if you go in. Check on site whether photos are allowed inside.
text.geographic_location: St. Lawrence's Church stands on Rua de São Lourenço in Macau, opposite the Instituto Salesiano.
text.directions_text: The church is opposite the Instituto Salesiano, which is a useful landmark when you arrive. From the street, climb the stone staircase through the palm garden to reach the front steps. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) on the steps. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot fit both bell towers in the frame. From the street below, the telephoto (2x) is useful for a tighter shot of the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there you get a symmetrical, raised view of the yellow and white facade and both bell towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and centre the doorway between the two towers so the symmetry shows. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. The palm garden the stairs lead into adds foreground interest. For an alternative, walk down to Rua de São Lourenço and photograph the whole facade and both towers from the street below the stair approach.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the yellow wall to set focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the white details do not wash out in bright light. Keep flash off, especially if you go inside.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Between about 5:00 and 6:30 PM, when the low sun warms the walls.

text.access_note: It is a working place of worship that is free to enter, but check opening hours locally before you go and keep quiet and avoid flash during Mass.

name: Lou Lim Ioc Garden
label: Lou Lim Ioc Garden
camera_source: Commons cluster (15 photos). Moved 78 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 55 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/265433531: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Lou Lim Ioc Park' (206 m across).
notes: Suzhou-style garden with a pond and pavilions.

text.description:
Lou Lim Ioc Garden is a small, calm park in the São Lázaro area of Macau, built in 1906 by a local merchant, Lou Kau, as part of his residence. Its design follows the well-known gardens of Suzhou, so you get a layered, almost painted look rather than open lawns. In 1974 it was handed to the Macau government and became a public park, and it is still popular with local people, so expect residents going about their day alongside visitors.

It photographs well because the Chinese-style layout works like a series of small scenes: water, planting, paths and garden buildings sit close together, and each turn gives you a fresh frame. Look for foreground interest, such as leaves, a railing or a bend in a path, with the garden stepping back behind it. Walk slowly and take several shots from different spots rather than one wide view.

On your phone, keep things simple. Use the gridlines to keep edges and rooflines straight, tap on your subject to set focus, and drag the exposure slider down a touch if bright sky is washing out the greenery. Please be considerate of people relaxing here when you are taking photos, especially if you want to include them in a portrait-style shot.
text.geographic_location: In the São Lázaro area of Macau. It was built as part of a merchant's residence and became a public park in 1974.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, rail or tram stops to give you here, so head for the São Lázaro area of Macau and ask locally for Lou Lim Ioc Garden. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for most views. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for tight paths or when you want to include more of the garden. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details such as roof edges or carved features.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Nine-Bend Bridge. The zigzag bridge crossing the lotus pond, framed by the water and surrounding greenery, with the bridge's angled sections leading the eye across the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the main feature on one third of the frame. Use a path, plant or railing in the foreground to give depth. Hold the phone level to keep straight lines true, and try one portrait-orientation shot as well as landscape.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the main subject to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if bright areas look too pale. Try a Live Photo to capture gentle movement in the water or leaves.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier in the day is usually calmer and gives you fewer people in the frame; soft, even light under the trees suits phone cameras well.

text.access_note: It is a public park, but opening arrangements can change, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The garden has water, planting, paths and garden buildings close together, typical of a Suzhou-style design.
Early in the day is usually quieter.
Light under the trees is typically soft and even, which suits phone cameras.
Opening arrangements for the park may change.

name: Sai Van Bridge
label: Sai Van Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Praça do Lago Sai Van' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '西灣湖廣場 Praça do Lago Sai Van' (way/243636989): middle (206 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/14071209: large area 'Sai Van Bridge' (2009 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Cable-stayed bridge linking the peninsula and Taipa.

text.description:
Sai Van Bridge is the long, curving cable-stayed bridge that links the Macau Peninsula with Taipa Island. It was opened on 19 December 2004 and is about 2.2 kilometres long. It was the third bridge built across the bay between the two. It has two decks, and the enclosed lower deck can stay in use when strong typhoons close the other two crossings. The lower deck also carries the Macau Light Transit System, which began running passengers on 8 December 2023.

For photographs, the best free view is from Praça do Lago Sai Van, at the lakeside end near the base of Macau Tower. When the water is calm, the lake can mirror the bridge, which is why guides point people here around dusk. You get a clear daytime shot first, then the night lighting as it gets dark.

If you have time for a second angle, Avenida da Minguo puts Macau Tower and the bridge together with the lake and city lights around them. Rua de Nossa Senhora da Penha, on the hill, gives a higher and wider view of the whole bridge with the tower rising behind it. Arrive a little before sunset so you can shoot in daylight, at twilight and after dark without moving far.
text.geographic_location: The bridge crosses the bay between the Macau Peninsula and Taipa Island. The recommended viewpoint, Praça do Lago Sai Van, is on the peninsula side beside the lake, near the base of Macau Tower.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so find Macau Tower on a map and walk to the lakeside square beside it. You do not need to walk to it, because the best view of the whole span is from the square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the bridge, lake and tower sit naturally together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the square and sky. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull Macau Tower and the bridge closer together.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Praça do Lago Sai Van (lakeside end, near the Macau Tower base). The bridge's S-shaped span across the lake, with Macau Tower and the city skyline in the same frame. Walk down towards the water's edge so the reflection is included.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the bridge along the lower third, with the reflection filling the bottom of the frame. Keep the horizon level so the span looks smooth. For a different view, try Avenida da Minguo, which puts the tower and bridge in one composition, or the hilltop street Rua de Nossa Senhora da Penha for a higher, wider view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lights do not blow out. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows on a railing or your body against a post to keep the phone still. A Live Photo can help catch a moment when the water is calm. Use panorama only if you can sweep slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Twilight is best. Arrive a little before sunset for clear daytime shots, then stay as the bridge lights come on and the calm lake reflects them.

text.access_note: Praça do Lago Sai Van is a public lakeside square with no ticket needed for the view; the Macau Tower observation deck is a separate paid attraction, so check the official site before you go if you want to go up.

name: Leal Senado Building
label: Leal Senado
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Largo do Senado' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '議事亭前地 Largo do Senado' (way/192573684): middle (131 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/192573674: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Leal Senado Building' (93 m across).
notes: Portuguese colonial municipal building on Senado Square.

text.description:
The Leal Senado is the old seat of Macau's government, and it stands at one end of Largo do Senado, the square at the heart of the Historic Centre. The name means 'Loyal Senate'. Portugal's prince regent gave Macau's government that title in 1810 as a reward for its loyalty to Portugal. The building went up after 1784, on the site of an earlier Chinese-style pavilion where Portuguese and Chinese officials used to meet. It is U-shaped, plain and restrained, and was part of the area added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2005. Today it houses Macau's municipal affairs office.

It photographs well because the square does so much of the work. From near the central fountain, the facade sits ahead of you with the wave-patterned pavement running towards it and the colonial fronts on either side. That gives a postcard view with plenty of depth, and a phone copes with it easily. The square is least crowded early in the morning, before about 10 AM, so an early start gives you cleaner frames with fewer people in them.

If you want something quieter, Travessa da Misericórdia gives a lower-angle side view of the street scene around the building, with colourful facades and shutters. Inside, the blue-and-white tile panels, the staircase and the courtyard garden make a different set of pictures. Photography is restricted in some exhibition areas and the library, so look for signs as you go.
text.geographic_location: In the São Lourenço area of Macau's Historic Centre, at one end of Largo do Senado (Senado Square).
text.directions_text: Head to the Largo do Senado area in the Historic Centre, and walk into the square towards the central fountain. From there the Leal Senado is to the south-west, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade and the patterned pavement in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the windows and the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Largo do Senado (near the central fountain, facing the south end where the building stands). The Leal Senado facade framed across the square with the wave-patterned pavement in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon of the pavement on the lower line, so the waves lead the eye up to the building. Keep the phone level, so the facade does not lean. For a quieter alternative with colourful facades and shutters, try a low-angle side view from Travessa da Misericórdia.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the building keeps its detail. Take a few shots in a row, since people keep walking through the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before about 10 AM, when the square is least crowded. Expect large crowds at weekends and at Chinese New Year.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the building is a working government office with exhibition areas and a library, so check the official site before you go for interior access and photography rules.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps fit the whole facade and foreground into one frame from the square.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep detail in the building when the sky is bright.

name: Our Lady of Penha Chapel, Macau
label: Penha Chapel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Miradouro de Nossa Senhora da Penha' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '西望洋聖母眺望台 Miradouro de Nossa Senhora da Penha' (way/643633778): middle (102 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/655240811: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Chapel of Our Lady of Penha' (54 m across).
notes: Hilltop chapel with views over the Inner Harbour.

text.description: Our Lady of Penha Chapel stands on top of Penha Hill on the Macau Peninsula, and it gives you two photographs in one visit. The pale white chapel with its bell tower looks good against a blue sky, and the hilltop terrace beside it looks out over the sea and the city. The first church here was built in 1622 by the crew of the Portuguese ship São Bartholomeu. They had escaped their Dutch pursuers and had promised to build a church if they got home safely. It was rebuilt in 1837 and then completely rebuilt in 1935 in the Neo-Manueline style, which is the building you see today. The same spot looks the other way towards the water. A Virgin Mary statue stands in the foreground, with Xiwang Lake, the cross-sea bridge and the Macau Tower and city skyline beyond. Take the chapel photo first, from the courtyard in front. Then walk to the railing for the skyline. The gardens around the chapel, with trees and benches, suit a quieter, closer picture. The hill is steep, so allow a little time and energy for the climb.
text.geographic_location: On Penha Hill in the São Lourenço area of the Macau Peninsula.
text.directions_text: Start from A-Ma Temple, which is about 15 minutes on foot from the hilltop. The hill is steep. Alternatively, take a taxi to the top. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the statue, sea and skyline together. Use the default lens (1x) for the chapel facade. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the Macau Tower closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Miradouro de Nossa Senhora da Penha (hilltop platform in front of the Virgin Mary statue, facing the sea). The Virgin statue in the foreground with Xiwang Lake, the cross-sea bridge and the Macau Tower and city skyline behind it. The chapel is just to the north-east, so turn round for it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the statue on one side and let the sea and skyline fill the rest. Rest your phone on the hilltop railing for a steadier skyline shot. For the chapel, walk to the courtyard in front and frame the white facade and bell tower against the sky. For a quieter, closer picture, use the garden with its trees and benches.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Switch on the gridlines to keep the horizon level. Tap the bright sky to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white chapel keeps its detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, around golden hour, is often recommended for this view.

text.access_note: The terrace and the outside of the chapel are open, but the chapel interior is often closed or limited to set hours, so check the current opening hours locally on the day before you go.

name: Mandarin's House
label: Mandarin's House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Largo do Lilau' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '亞婆井前地 Largo do Lilau' (way/206830675): middle (67 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/404235920: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Mandarin's House' (132 m across).
notes: Traditional Chinese family compound from the 19th century.

text.description:
The Mandarin's House is a large historic family home in the São Lourenço area of Macau. It was the home of Zheng Guanying (1842–1921), a late Qing writer and reformer who finished his best-known book, Shengshi Weiyan, here. The house was built in 1869 by his father, Zheng Wenrui, and the family went on adding to it. It covers about 4,000 square metres, which makes it one of the largest family houses in Macau. The style is mostly Cantonese, with some western touches mixed in. It became part of the Historic Centre of Macau, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, in 2005.

For photographs, the quieter choice is Largo do Lilau, the small square behind the house. It usually makes a calmer, more artistic picture than the busy entrance. If you have time, the gate and front of the house, framed by the doorway with the courtyard beyond, make a good second shot. Take a few frames from the square first, then step closer for details such as brickwork, doors and roof edges. Inside, photography is not allowed in some areas, and flash and touching the furniture are discouraged. Check the signs as you go.
text.geographic_location: The Mandarin's House is in the São Lourenço area of Macau, in the old part of the city, and is part of the Historic Centre of Macau UNESCO World Heritage Site.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stops are listed for this spot, so it is best reached on foot from the São Lourenço area. Walk to the Mandarin's House (Casa do Mandarim), then continue to Largo do Lilau on the side facing the back of the mansion. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the rear of the house from the square. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough to fit the walls in. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for brickwork, windows and roof details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Largo do Lilau (behind the house, on the side facing the back of the mansion). The rear of the Mandarin's House seen from the adjoining plaza, useful for a more artistic, less crowded composition. From here you look west at the rear of the mansion. This is a quieter view than the entrance and suits a more artistic composition.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the long wall along a lower grid line, keeping the verticals straight. Include a little of the square in the foreground to give a sense of place. For a second picture, go to the entrance and frame the gate and front of the house, with the courtyard visible beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the grey brick keeps its detail. Do not use flash inside.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No best time is documented for this spot. Wherever you stand, check the house's visiting days before you go.

text.access_note: The house is a heritage site with an interior, and its closing day and entry details can vary, so check on the day and on the official site before you go; some interior areas do not allow photography or flash, while Largo do Lilau is an open public square.
claims_not_in_sources: The square behind the house is usually quieter than the entrance.
The ultra-wide lens helps if you cannot step back far enough in the square.
